source.title: Artificial Neural Variability for Deep Learning: On Overfitting, Noise Memorization, and Catastrophic Forgetting
source.authors: Zeke Xie; Fengxiang He; Shaopeng Fu; Issei Sato; D. Tao; Masashi Sugiyama

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices and supplementary results.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether an added weight-perturbation training method changes generalization gaps, using a different intervention from the listed original studies. It also reports robustness to corrupted-label memorization, but does not test the claim's random-label capacity result.
record.gate_note: The paper reports outcomes for NVRM, PSGD, optimizer comparisons, and weight perturbation. Cited findings about random-label fitting and prior methods are not this study's results. Figure-based curves lack extractable exact values, so qualitative text reports are recorded as text results; exact curve values are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The study uses flatness–generalization arguments to motivate NVRM and evaluates its own method. It does not test V7's magnitude-scaled perturbation measure or its ranking of generalization gaps: Experiment 1 measures test accuracy under unscaled weight noise, while Experiment 2 measures gaps in different architectures. None of its results tests another listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' conclusion: they argue that ANV regularizes information in learned weights and report that NVRM improves weight-perturbation robustness, generalization, noisy-label robustness and continual-task retention. Negligible computational and coding costs are their stated claim, rather than a quantified cost comparison in these rows.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces weight perturbations during gradient evaluation and a de-noising step at inference/training updates; compares with standard SGD/Adam. Experiments use conventional architectures, datasets, augmentation, weight decay, and schedules.
record.method_sensitivity: NVRM variability scale, noise type, architecture, dataset, and learning rate are varied in reported experiments; the authors state Gaussian is nearly one point better at its optimum while uniform is more robust across variability scales.

fits_no_version.finding: NVRM-trained ResNet-34 models retain test accuracy under unscaled isotropic Gaussian weight noise better than SGD-trained models; the authors describe lower expected sharpness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NVRM improves test-accuracy robustness to unscaled weight perturbations in the tested image classifiers.

fits_no_version.finding: NVRM reduces the training–test accuracy gap and slightly improves test accuracy for VGG-16 on CIFAR-10 and MobileNetV2 on CIFAR-100.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NVRM can reduce generalization gaps and improve held-out accuracy in these training settings.

fits_no_version.finding: NVRM mitigates corrupted-label fitting; its performance depends on noise distribution and variability scale. Larger SGD learning rates slow memorization but do not prevent its eventual occurrence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NVRM improves robustness to partial label corruption relative to the tested SGD and PSGD baselines.

fits_no_version.finding: NVRM-Adam improves retention across Permuted MNIST tasks and enhances EWC.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NVRM can mitigate catastrophic forgetting in the tested continual-learning settings.

record.problems: Relevant comparison curves are mostly figure-only and lack exact values in the supplied text. Mean performance and standard deviations over 10 trials are stated generally, but condition-specific uncertainty is not available in the extracted text. No random-label fitting experiment is conducted.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible results were omitted. Figure-only conditions were not expanded into separate rows where the text did not identify their individual values or conditions.

untested.parts: Matched natural-label and fixed random-label training, near-perfect random-label fitting, and the corresponding held-out accuracies.
Test-error behavior as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier performance and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning, optimizer switching, and decoupled weight decay.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe changes that reduce their penalty.
Dropout effects across training-set sizes, dropout strengths, augmentation and weight-decay settings.

Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance measured through training error, its association with generalization gaps among similarly fitted networks, and its ranking relative to norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing examples selected by memorization scores, retraining, and comparing test-accuracy losses with matched random removals.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because the measured outcomes fit none of those versions; this does not negate the reported method improvements. The theoretical bounds concern unscaled Gaussian perturbations under stated assumptions and do not establish V7's empirical ranking claim. Supplementary Figures 8, 9 and 12 add method results outside the versions, so they do not require version-linked missing entries.

versions.untested_parts: Does not train on randomly labelled data or report natural-label held-out accuracy alongside random-label held-out accuracy.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold test.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison on image or language benchmarks.
Tests robustness to unscaled isotropic Gaussian weight perturbation and reports expected minima sharpness, but does not compare magnitude-aware sharpness against norm- and margin-based measures.
Does not remove memorized examples or compare removal against random-example removal.

rows.subject: ResNet-34
rows.operation_detail: Test accuracy under isotropic Gaussian perturbation of all weights across noise scales.
rows.measure: Test accuracy under weight perturbation; expected minima sharpness is also described qualitatively.
rows.value: Figure-only curves; text says SGD-trained network has nearly lost all learned knowledge due to relatively large weight noise.
rows.note: The text does not quantify the perturbation tolerance or provide the corresponding accuracy values for SGD.
rows.check: Unscaled Gaussian perturbations evaluated using test accuracy cannot establish V7's relation between magnitude-aware training-error sharpness and generalization gaps.

rows.subject: ResNet-34
rows.operation_detail: Compared NVRM-SGD and SGD on noisy-label training; tracked training and test accuracy over epochs.
rows.measure: Training and test accuracy over epochs
rows.value: Text says SGD almost memorizes all noisy labels while NVRM almost only learns clean labels; NVRM stops learning when training error is close to the label noise rate.
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviations over 10 trials are described generally; figure-specific uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: Corrupted-label memorization is not random-label fit or natural-label held-out generalization as named by V1.
rows.check: Partial asymmetric label corruption does not test V1's matched natural-label versus fixed random-label experiment. This is a noisy-label mitigation comparison.

rows.subject: ResNet-34
rows.operation_detail: Compared NVRM-SGD and SGD on noisy-label training; tracked test accuracy over epochs.
rows.value: Text says NVRM with default b = 0.05 can significantly relieve memorizing noisy labels; exact values are figure-only.
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviations over 10 trials are described generally; figure-specific uncertainty not stated.
rows.note: Corrupted-label memorization is not random-label fit or natural-label held-out generalization as named by V1.
rows.check: This noisy-label mitigation result does not test V1. Figure 3 also reports CIFAR-100 training accuracy, which the row's operation and measure omit.

rows.subject: Three-layer Fully-Connected Network (FCN)

rows.measure: Base-task accuracy and mean accuracy of learned tasks after each task
rows.value: Text says NVRM forgets knowledge from previous tasks much slower; exact values are figure-only.
rows.note: Catastrophic forgetting is explicitly outside the claim's in-distribution generalization versions.
rows.check: Continual-task retention is outside the listed versions. Figure 4 varies variability scale after five tasks; Figure 11 reports accuracy against task count.

rows.subject: Three-layer Fully-Connected Network (FCN)
rows.size_stated: two hidden layers and 1024 ReLUs per hidden layer
rows.operation_detail: Compared EWC and EWC combined with NVRM-Adam across tasks.

rows.value: Text says NVRM enhances EWC effectively; exact values are figure-only.
rows.note: Catastrophic forgetting is explicitly outside the claim's in-distribution generalization versions.
rows.check: EWC enhancement is outside the listed versions. The source is inconsistent: Figure 5 specifies importance values 300 and 1000, while Appendix C.2 specifies 30 and 1000.

rows.subject: ResNet34
rows.operation_detail: Compared PSGD, NVRM-SGD, and SGD across weight-noise scales.
rows.value: Text says PSGD may prevent memorizing noisy labels much better than SGD, while NVRM still outperforms PSGD significantly by nearly seven points.
rows.note: The comparison is reported qualitatively; no exact curves or values are supplied.
rows.check: Comparison of NVRM, PSGD and SGD on corrupted labels measures mitigation performance, not a listed version. The nearly seven-point improvement does not warrant a partial state for any version.

rows.subject: ResNet34
rows.operation_detail: Compared Gaussian-, Laplace-, and uniform-noise NVRM-SGD across variability scales.
rows.value: Text says all three types achieve remarkable improvements over SGD; optimal Gaussian test performance is nearly one point better than uniform and Laplace, while uniform is more robust to variability scale.
rows.note: Noise type changes the reported outcome; the text gives qualitative comparisons but not exact test-error values.
rows.check: Noise-distribution tuning of NVRM is outside the listed versions. Figure 7 plots test accuracy, although the surrounding prose calls the plotted quantity test error; record this source inconsistency.

rows.subject: ResNet-34
rows.operation_detail: Compared NVRM-SGD and SGD on symmetric noisy-label training.
rows.value: Appendix says results demonstrate NVRM can significantly improve robustness to symmetric label noise; exact values are figure-only.
rows.note: The text reports a pooled qualitative conclusion over the stated datasets and rates; it does not give per-condition numerical values.
rows.check: Symmetric partial label corruption and its mitigation do not supply V1's matched natural-label and fully random-label results.

rows.subject: SGD
rows.operation_detail: Compared SGD at learning rates 0.1, 0.3, 1, and 3 with NVRM-SGD.
rows.measure: Training accuracy and test accuracy over epochs
rows.value: Text says SGD with larger stochastic gradient noise memorizes noisy labels more slowly but still memorizes nearly all noisy labels at the final phase.
rows.note: This is a negative result about noisy-label memorization and is not a versioned claim outcome.
rows.check: SGD is an optimizer, not a model subject. This learning-rate comparison does not vary batch size or test V5; Figure 13 uses learning-rate reductions every 60 epochs.

rows.subject: NVRM-SGD
rows.operation_detail: Compared NVRM-SGD at learning rates 0.1, 0.3, 1, and 3 with SGD.
rows.measure: Training accuracy and test accuracy over epochs
rows.value: Text says NVRM-SGD with various learning rates can consistently relieve overfitting noisy labels.
rows.note: This is a noisy-label result, not random-label memorization or natural-label generalization.
rows.check: NVRM-SGD names the training method rather than the network subject. This noisy-label mitigation comparison tests no listed version; Figure 13 uses learning-rate reductions every 60 epochs.
